articles.title: Black Friday Cyber Threats — Part Two: Retailers
articles.context: In Part One of our Black Friday Cyber Threats blog series, we examined how Black Friday creates opportunities for attackers to target consumers through fraud, impersonation,...
articles.full_text:
In Part One of our Black Friday Cyber Threats blog series, we examined how Black Friday creates opportunities for attackers to target consumers through fraud, impersonation, credential theft, and malware. Retailers experience many of those same threats at scale, while also contending with bot activity, business-logic abuse, operational disruption, and growing questions around AI-driven commerce.

The same conditions that make Cyber Week commercially successful, including intense demand, compressed decision-making, and massive volumes of online activity, also create opportunities for attackers to exploit both technical weaknesses and business processes at scale.

Black Friday therefore amplifies five security challenges that retailers already face throughout the year:

Automated traffic and inventory abuse: Bots drive a substantial share of seasonal online activity, creating risks ranging from credential attacks and promotional abuse to inventory hoarding, scraping, fraudulent transactions, and operational disruption.

Account takeover and authenticated-session abuse: Compromised customer accounts can expose payment methods, loyalty balances, customer information, and post-purchase workflows, while stolen browser sessions may allow attackers to operate from contexts the retailer already trusts.

Business-logic abuse: Automation enables attackers to target coupons, gift cards, loyalty programs, refunds, returns, inventory reservations, and customer-service processes at a scale that is difficult to detect through traditional fraud controls alone.

Availability and operational disruption: Peak shopping periods reduce tolerance for outages, false positives, and manual review, creating opportunities for bot-driven attacks, credential campaigns, and denial-of-service activity to affect business operations during critical revenue periods.

Data theft and extortion: Holiday trading periods concentrate revenue and operational dependence into a short timeframe, increasing the potential impact of ransomware, data theft, and extortion attempts timed to coincide with periods of heightened business pressure.

AI is influencing this environment in two distinct ways:

Generative AI enables attackers to create more convincing phishing campaigns, fraudulent listings, fake reviews, social-engineering content, and other forms of deception at greater speed and scale.

Agentic commerce introduces autonomous software capable of researching products, comparing options, and completing purchases on behalf of consumers, creating new challenges around identity, authorization, trust, and fraud prevention.

Recent incident response data suggest attackers are operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations have not previously encountered. Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record in October 2026, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf rising 78%, as well as network intrusion cases, including ransomware, rising 96% compared with typical monthly volumes. Those trends point to a threat environment where adversaries are increasingly using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

The emergence of shopping agents adds another layer of complexity. Retailers are beginning to encounter situations where software, rather than a human customer, may be browsing products, comparing prices, authenticating to accounts, and completing transactions. Traditional fraud controls often rely on indicators such as browsing behavior, transaction velocity, device characteristics, and network origin to distinguish legitimate shoppers from malicious automation. As agentic commerce expands, those signals become less reliable, forcing retailers to determine not only whether a customer and payment method are legitimate, but also whether the software acting on the customer’s behalf is authorized to do so.

Black Friday therefore serves as a practical example of how cyber threats are evolving. Attackers do not need entirely new techniques to increase risk. They can achieve significant impact by combining automation, AI, credential theft, fraud, and business-process abuse with the predictable operational pressures that accompany major retail events. At the same time, retailers must adapt to a future where a growing share of legitimate commercial activity may also be automated, making trust, attribution, and verification increasingly important components of security and fraud prevention.

How AI, Automation, and Fraud Are Reshaping Retail Cyber Risk

1. Automated traffic and inventory abuse

Retailers have been managing automated traffic for years, long before the current conversation around AI shopping assistants. Against that backdrop, attackers are using AI to test stolen credentials, scrape inventory data, abuse promotions, hoard high-demand products, and facilitate fraud at a scale that would be difficult to achieve manually. For retailers, the operational challenge is understanding who is behind that activity, what they are attempting to accomplish, and whether their actions align with the interests of the business and its customers.

The holiday shopping season increases the complexity. More customers are online, transaction volumes climb, and activity extends well beyond traditional business hours. Based on aggregated telemetry across our customer base, roughly 44% of alerts arrive outside the standard workday, which means a substantial portion of potential threats emerge overnight, on weekends, and during holiday periods when response teams have historically had fewer resources available.

Security teams are increasingly turning to AI to help manage that reality. As the volume of activity grows, organizations need the ability to evaluate alerts, identify suspicious behavior, correlate signals across systems, and begin investigations without waiting for someone to come online. During high-volume periods such as Black Friday and Cyber Monday, that speed becomes particularly valuable because attackers can move from initial access to follow-on activity in a matter of minutes.

Retail organizations appear to recognize that shift. In Arctic Wolf’s 2026 AI & Cybersecurity Trends Report, 95% of retail respondents reported having 24×7 monitoring coverage, the highest level of any industry surveyed. The same respondents identified secure AI adoption and preparing for the pace of AI-driven change as their top priorities over the next year, reflecting a broader understanding that both commerce and cyber threats are becoming faster, more automated, and more difficult to evaluate through human effort alone.

2. Agent identity creates a fraud-control dilemma

Agentic commerce introduces a new identity challenge for retailers because software, rather than a customer, may be navigating the shopping experience and completing transactions on the customer’s behalf.

Many fraud-detection systems were designed around assumptions about human behavior, evaluating factors such as browsing patterns, device identity, network origin, and checkout activity to determine whether a transaction appears legitimate. Authorized shopping agents may not behave like traditional customers. They may move through a site rapidly, skip intermediate steps, or operate through shared cloud infrastructure. At the same time, malicious actors are likely to adapt their own automation to resemble legitimate agents.

As a result, retailers will need new ways to establish trust, verify authorization, and maintain accountability throughout the purchasing process. The challenge extends beyond fraud prevention to questions of attribution, auditability, and dispute resolution when a transaction is later challenged by a customer.

3. Product and content manipulation

AI shopping agents rely on information they find across the internet, including product descriptions, reviews, advertisements, search results, and retailer websites. That means attackers don’t necessarily have to target the shopper directly. In some cases, influencing the information an agent sees may be enough.

A compromised product feed could direct customers to the wrong destination or display inaccurate pricing and inventory information. Fraudulent listings could be designed to appear more attractive to recommendation engines. Reviews and other user-generated content may become vehicles for manipulation, particularly if shopping agents begin relying on them more heavily when making recommendations or purchase decisions.

These aren’t entirely new problems. Retailers have spent years dealing with fake reviews, search manipulation, fraudulent listings, and advertising abuse. The difference is that AI shopping agents may consume and act on that information much faster than a human shopper would, increasing the importance of ensuring that the underlying data is accurate and trustworthy.

4. Account takeover and authenticated-session abuse

Compromised retail accounts have long been valuable to attackers because they often provide access to saved payment methods, loyalty balances, order histories, and customer account settings. The risk increases when attackers gain access to an authenticated browser session or shopping agent session, allowing them to operate from a context the retailer may already recognize as trusted.

Once inside an account, attackers can steal loyalty points and gift cards, redirect shipments, abuse promotions, initiate fraudulent purchases, manipulate refunds, or exploit trusted access to customer and supplier portals. Many of these activities can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate account activity because they occur after a successful login.

ClickFix campaigns add another dimension to this risk. Information-stealing malware is designed to collect browser credentials, session tokens, authentication artifacts, and other sensitive data that help attackers bypass traditional login controls. What begins as a consumer-focused lure can therefore have broader consequences if the compromised device belongs to an employee with access to corporate systems, supplier relationships, or business applications. In those cases, an account-compromise event can become an entry point into a much larger environment.

5. Business-logic abuse at scale

Retailers should expect automated abuse to extend well beyond payment fraud. The same technologies that help shoppers move more quickly through the buying process can also be used to exploit promotions, reserve inventory, test gift card balances, manipulate loyalty accounts, automate refund requests, and target customer service teams with convincing social engineering schemes. As more retail activity becomes digital, attackers gain additional opportunities to operate at a speed and scale that can be difficult to detect through human review alone.

At the same time, AI-powered shopping assistants are beginning to take on a greater role throughout the customer journey, from product discovery and recommendations to transaction support and post-purchase interactions. That shift introduces new challenges around identity, trust, and fraud prevention. Retailers will increasingly need to distinguish between legitimate automated activity acting on behalf of customers and malicious automation designed to abuse systems, manipulate transactions, or gain unauthorized access to accounts and services.

6. Availability and operational risk

Peak shopping periods create a difficult balancing act for retailers. Customers expect fast transactions, immediate access to promotions, and uninterrupted service, leaving little tolerance for outages, delays, or excessive verification steps. Threat actors understand that pressure and may try to exploit it through bot activity, credential attacks, fraud campaigns, and other forms of malicious automation designed to blend into legitimate customer traffic.

Recent Arctic Wolf incident response data suggests attackers are already operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations are struggling to manage. In October 2026, the Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf increasing 78% compared with typical monthly volumes. While that increase was not specific to retail organizations or Black Friday activity, it reflects a broader threat environment in which adversaries are using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

7. Data Theft and Extortion Exploit Peak Operating Pressure

Black Friday concentrates transaction volume and revenue into a period when retailers have little tolerance for disruption. Threat actors can exploit that operational pressure by timing ransomware deployment, data theft, or extortion demands for holiday weekends, when response capacity may be reduced and every hour of downtime carries greater commercial impact.

The FBI and CISA have previously observed highly disruptive ransomware attacks occurring on holidays and weekends, when limited network-defense and IT capacity can give attackers additional time to expand access and deploy ransomware. Their guidance does not identify a Black Friday-specific campaign, but the underlying conditions are directly applicable to retailers operating through Thanksgiving weekend.

Modern extortion also does not require encryption. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security warns that threat actors increasingly use stolen data as the primary source of leverage, threatening disclosure or destruction even when the victim can restore systems from backups. Potential retail exposure includes customer and employee data, payment-related information, supplier records, contracts, pricing data, loyalty accounts, and internal communications.

Before Cyber Week begins, retailers should focus on controlling who and what can transact in their environment. That means distinguishing trusted shopping agents from malicious automation, strengthening authentication for high-risk actions like loyalty redemptions and address changes, and maintaining clear records of customer authorization. As AI-powered commerce grows, proving who approved a purchase may become just as important as processing the payment.

Retailers should remember that the fundamentals have not changed. Visibility, identity security, continuous monitoring, and tested response processes remain the foundation of resilience. What has changed is the speed at which attackers can operate.

Arctic Wolf’s recent incident response data and Agentic Security Operations research suggest adversaries are increasingly using automation and AI to scale familiar attack techniques. As a result, organizations need the ability to detect, investigate, and respond at machine speed while maintaining human oversight of critical decisions. The most likely Black Friday threats remain account takeover, phishing, payment fraud, malware, and business-logic abuse, but AI is making those attacks faster, easier to scale, and harder to distinguish from legitimate activity.

articles.title: Black Friday Cyber Threats — Part One: Consumers
articles.context: Fraud, credential theft, malware delivery, and social engineering all benefit when attackers can blend into trusted experiences and exploit moments when people are moving quickly
articles.full_text:
For millions of consumers globally, Black Friday creates exactly the kind of environment cybercriminals look for when assessing their targets, which is urgency, high transaction volume, and people clicking links, tracking packages, and hunting for deals. Rather than introducing new threats, Black Friday amplifies four risk categories that security teams already contend with year-round:

Fraud and impersonation: Fake retailers, brand-spoofing sites, fraudulent advertisements, delivery messages, and account-support scams remain the most immediate consumer threats.

Credential and session theft: Phishing, account takeover, and information-stealing malware can expose retail accounts, payment information, email, loyalty balances, and authenticated browser sessions.

Malware delivery: ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA techniques can turn shopping, coupon, and delivery lures into endpoint compromise.

Automated and agentic activity: Retailers must distinguish legitimate customers and authorized shopping agents from inventory bots, account-abuse automation, and fraud infrastructure.

AI amplifies this environment in two different ways: 1. AI can improve the quality, localization, and scale of fraudulent content and 2. Shopping agents can shorten the path from product discovery to payment.

Recent incident response data suggest attackers are operating at a level of speed and scale that many organizations have not previously encountered. Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Incident Response team experienced its busiest month on record in October 2026, with cases from organizations not protected by Arctic Wolf rising 78%, as well as network intrusion cases, including ransomware, rising 96% compared with previous months in 2026. Those trends point to a threat environment where adversaries are using automation and AI to make established attack techniques more efficient, more targeted, and easier to deploy at scale.

As transaction volume rises and shoppers make faster decisions, phishing, impersonation, credential theft, and account-takeover activity become more likely to blend into normal behavior. Black Friday therefore serves as a useful case study in how modern cyber threats evolve. Attackers do not always need new techniques. They often achieve greater impact simply by combining trusted brands, social engineering, automation, and AI to exploit predictable moments of consumer urgency.

Threats to Consumers

1. Fake stores, impersonation, and payment fraud

Consumers remain most likely to encounter fraudulent retailers, counterfeit products, deceptive advertisements, phishing messages, and false delivery notifications. The immediate objectives are usually to obtain payment, harvest credentials, collect personal information, or redirect the victim to another scam.

The large increase in overall fraud losses does not establish an equivalent increase in shopping fraud. FBI data shows that investment, business email compromise, and support fraud produced considerably higher losses than non-delivery and credit card fraud in 2025. The key takeaway is that online shopping fraud remains highly relevant during Black Friday, not that it is driving the overall increase in reported fraud losses.

2. ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA malware delivery

Some holiday scams may be looking for far more than payment information. One technique defenders are watching closely is ClickFix, a social engineering tactic that presents what appears to be a legitimate CAPTCHA, browser error, document issue, or verification step. Instead of solving a problem, the victim is instructed to copy, paste, and run a command through PowerShell, Windows Run, Command Prompt, or Terminal, effectively launching the attack themselves. Arctic Wolf has tracked the technique across multiple campaigns, including a ClickFix campaign that used an obfuscated PowerShell loader to facilitate malicious activity, a fake CAPTCHA lure delivering PsyloStealer, and the FileFix delivery method used to distribute Interlock RAT.

The approach is effective because it blends into everyday online activity. During Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, attackers have no shortage of believable scenarios to work with. A fake shopping site might ask visitors to verify they are human before accessing a limited-time sale, claim a browser extension is required to activate a coupon, or display a message saying a package tracking page, invoice, or payment verification process cannot continue until a quick troubleshooting step is completed. Those instructions ultimately direct the victim to run a command that can install malware or provide attackers with access to credentials, sensitive files, or enterprise systems.

While there is no specific reporting showing a surge in ClickFix activity tied directly to Black Friday, the technique has become an increasingly common part of the threat landscape. The success of campaigns such as those documented in Arctic Wolf’s ClickFix, PsyloStealer, and FileFix investigations demonstrates how easily threat actors can disguise malicious requests as routine troubleshooting steps. The volume of holiday shopping, package tracking, promotional emails, and payment-related activity during the season creates even more opportunities to hide those requests inside workflows that users already trust.

3. Account takeover and information theft

Compromised email accounts can enable attackers to reset passwords, intercept order confirmations, redirect deliveries, and identify other linked financial services. Stolen browser cookies and authentication tokens can further extend access by allowing attackers to hijack authenticated sessions and, in some cases, bypass password-based controls.

Black Friday increases the practical value of compromised retail accounts because they may contain:

Stored payment methods

Loyalty points and rewards

Gift-card balances

Order histories

Saved delivery addresses

Active authenticated sessions

4. AI-assisted social engineering

AI-generated text, images, advertisements, and fictitious profiles allow scammers to produce polished, localized campaigns rapidly across brands, countries, products, and delivery providers. Social media provides a high-volume distribution channel for this content: nearly 30% of consumers reporting a fraud loss in 2025 said the scam began on social media, and shopping scams accounted for more than 40% of those reports, per the FTC. The FBI has also documented criminals using generative AI to create fictitious profiles, targeted messages, celebrity endorsements, and counterfeit-product promotions at scale.

Consumers should therefore rely less on writing quality as a trust signal and more on behavioral indicators:

Unexpected urgency

Extreme discounts

Pressure to leave an official platform

Requests for cryptocurrency, gift cards, or bank transfers

Unfamiliar merchant domains

Requests to install software or browser extensions

Instructions to paste commands into system tools

5. Personal shopping agents

Personal AI agents can now browse products and complete portions of the transaction process. According to Stripe, Meta’s Muse can check out at more than one million Link-enabled businesses and can use a single-use virtual card elsewhere. The consumer is required to approve each transaction total, and Muse does not receive the underlying payment details.

Payment controls like these reduce credential exposure. Approving a transaction amount doesn’t by itself confirm the consumer is buying from the intended merchant or getting the intended product. A consumer could approve the expected amount while failing to recognize an impersonation site, counterfeit item, manipulated listing, or fraudulent seller.

Fraud, credential theft, malware delivery, and social engineering all benefit when attackers can blend into trusted experiences and exploit moments when people are moving quickly. The most effective scams rarely depend on sophisticated technical exploits. Instead, they rely on convincing users to trust a familiar brand, click a timely message, approve a transaction, install software, or follow instructions that appear legitimate. AI is making those interactions more polished and easier to scale.

Organizations focused on protecting customers and reducing cyber risk can strengthen their security posture by combining user awareness with continuous monitoring, threat detection, and incident response capabilities that help identify and contain threats before they become significant security events.

As attackers increasingly use automation and AI to accelerate established tactics, security operations must operate with greater speed, visibility, and context. Arctic Wolf helps organizations improve cyber resilience through the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, which combines human expertise with AI-driven security operations, threat intelligence, and incident response to help security teams detect, investigate, and respond to threats faster. With the Aurora Agentic SOC extending security operations through autonomous and human-guided workflows, organizations are better positioned to keep pace with an increasingly fast-moving threat landscape.

-Justin Moore, Director of Adversary Operations, Arctic Wolf

articles.title: Incident Response at Machine Speed: What Black October’s Record Case Volume Reveals About Today’s Threat Landscape
articles.context: Organizations are also rapidly adopting AI tools, integrations, and services of their own, expanding the attack surface that their adversaries could exploit
articles.full_text:
The scale and severity of cybersecurity activity in October 2026 was unprecedented. Arctic Wolf Aurora Incident Response handled 78% more non-Arctic Wolf customer cases than the average month, and sophisticated network intrusion incidents, including ransomware, for non-Arctic Wolf customers rose by 96%, accounting for nearly all of the growth. Attackers aren’t just more active. They’re more dangerous.

But given how quickly the threat landscape is changing, October being our busiest month on record for our Aurora Incident Response team isn’t an anomaly, but rather the start of a new normal.

With a growing volume of disclosed vulnerabilities and the speed with which attackers are exploiting them, defenders should not expect conditions to become less demanding anytime soon.

As we saw from the PHP2Shell and Java4Shell disclosures that dominated recent headlines, attackers appear to be using AI to research targets, identify vulnerabilities, create phishing lures, and run campaigns at a scale that wasn’t possible just a few months ago. Organizations are also rapidly adopting AI tools, integrations, and services of their own, expanding the attack surface that their adversaries could exploit. Together, these behaviors are contributing to a higher volume of incidents and creating more opportunities for attackers to gain access.

From AI-Enabled Attackers to AI-Enabled Malware

But it’s not just AI adoption, or using AI to develop threat tactics and techniques, that is creating this frictionless environment for attackers. Malware itself is starting to use AI during attacks. Rather than carrying all of its instructions from the start, some malware now includes a lightweight loader that reaches out to an LLM for guidance while it runs. In Arctic Wolf’s malware samples we analyzed, we observed Large Language Model (LLM) API calls during execution, showing that AI is increasingly becoming part of the attack chain itself, not just a tool attackers use beforehand.

Today, these uses are relatively simple. We’ve seen malware use LLMs to generate file names, customize payloads, and create convincing social engineering messages on demand. But the same approach could evolve to support more advanced capabilities, such as adapting to security controls, tailoring attacks to specific victims, or helping attackers navigate an environment after initial access.

That creates a challenge for defenders. Traditional malware detections focus on what’s stored on disk, which means they can miss logic delivered in real time through an AI service. In order to build resilience against these kinds of AI-embedded malware, defenders need to monitor runtime behavior more closely, including unexpected processes making outbound connections to LLM platforms or AI APIs. This requires organizations to have full visibility into their environment.

AI has already changed the threat landscape by making sophisticated attacks easier to pull off. Techniques that once required deep expertise are now within reach for a much wider range of attackers, and those attackers can operate at a faster pace and larger scale than ever before. October’s incident data reflects that shift.

For our non-Arctic Wolf customers, business email compromise (BEC) incidents remained relatively steady, but more complex attacks surged. Ransomware cases rose by 77%, pre-ransomware cases rose by 55% and network intrusion incidents as a whole rose 96%.

These advances suggest that as more threat actors gain access to advanced capabilities, organizations are facing a growing volume of serious and potentially damaging attacks. Thankfully, we have insight into who these newly resource-enabled attackers are targeting, how they’re tailoring their attack patterns, and which threat groups are the most active.

More Attackers, More Opportunities for Compromised

The attack patterns observed in October reflect the reality that social engineering, external remote access, and exploitation of internet-facing systems were the most common attack vectors in Aurora Incident Response engagements. AI is helping attackers make these techniques more effective. Phishing messages can be personalized in seconds. Reconnaissance that once took days can be completed in minutes. Attackers can scan large portions of the internet for vulnerable systems and quickly focus their efforts on organizations that appear easiest to compromise.

The ransomware groups most frequently observed in October included Akira, Qilin, INC, DragonForce, and Settra.1 Organizations across legal services, manufacturing, real estate, software development, and financial services accounted for the largest share of incident response cases. These industries continue to attract attacker attention because of the sensitive data they manage, the operational disruption they can suffer, and the financial leverage they often present during an attack.

Organizations do not need to slow AI adoption, but they do need to prepare for an environment where attackers can operate at machine speed. Understanding internet-facing assets, maintaining strong identity controls, reducing unnecessary exposure, and regularly testing incident response plans all become more important as the pace of attacks increases.

Cyber resilience depends on knowing how to respond when prevention fails. The organizations that recover fastest are often the ones that prepared before the incident occurred, established clear escalation paths, and practiced how they would respond under pressure.

1 Threat actor attribution reflects Arctic Wolf’s assessment based on October 2026 incident data and may evolve with new evidence. References to threat actor identity are analytical judgments, not statements of legal fact.

This blog reflects my own views as of the publication date and includes forward-looking statements about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

articles.title: AI-Driven Attacks Are Here. Five Steps CISOs Should Take Now
articles.context: This open-source attack framework works with almost any LLM, and threat actors began experimenting with it against organizations within weeks of its release
articles.full_text:
Earlier this year, Claude Mythos Preview showed the security community what a frontier AI model can do when it’s pointed at software, finding and linking vulnerabilities far faster than defenders had ever seen up to that point. Access to that model stayed tightly controlled, but ARTEX has recently removed that corporate barrier for attackers. This open-source attack framework works with almost any LLM, and threat actors began experimenting with it against organizations within weeks of its release.

Although the developer later removed the project from GitHub, the code was quickly mirrored elsewhere and remains accessible. More importantly, we’re seeing these techniques attempted against customers. Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, including AntiFox, operating from public cloud infrastructure. In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were linked to confirmed malicious activity targeting internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.1 There is no indication the hosting provider was aware of or involved in this activity.

We’re seeing the effects of these enhanced offensive AI capabilities in our own case data. In what some industry leaders are calling ‘Black October’ due to the spike in vulnerability disclosures and threat activity, Arctic Wolf Aurora Incident Response handled 78% more non-Arctic Wolf customer cases than the average month prior, and although Business email compromise (BEC) activity remained relatively flat, more complex attacks surged. Network intrusion attacks, including ransomware, rose by 96%, meaning that attackers aren’t just more active. They’re more dangerous.

CISOs know AI is changing the threat landscape, and our case data reflects that shift. To adapt their security operations to keep pace with this shift, security teams should focus on five areas.

Reset Your Response Timelines

Most incident response plans created pre-AI, or even prior to this year, assume there will be enough time to assess what’s happening, gather the right stakeholders, and make containment decisions before an attacker causes significant damage. Increasingly, that’s not the case, especially in large organizations with long chains of approval. Because AI is helping attackers move faster, organizations need to remove as much friction from their response plan as possible, which means deciding in advance how a security team can take action without waiting for approval.

Map Everything Attackers Can See

AI-driven tools can scan thousands of potential targets at once and quickly identify the easiest path into an environment. That’s why there’s never been a better time for defenders to take full inventory of what systems, applications, and services they use are exposed to the internet. With a full inventory, security teams can prioritize taking action on the exposures that are likely to be targeted first.

Strengthen Identity Controls

Social engineering and external remote access ranked among the most common attack vectors in our October engagements, and AI is making both easier to execute at scale. An attacker can now generate extremely convincing phishing messages, and thus targeted campaigns, in seconds using publicly available information. That makes strong identity controls absolutely critical in today’s security landscape. Organizations should prioritize phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, regularly review their remote access tools and old or inactive accounts, as well as apply the same level of scrutiny to their service accounts and API keys. Those often carry extensive permissions but receive far less oversight than human users, making them an attractive target for attackers.

Monitor Behavior at Runtime

Some malware now contacts an LLM during execution to retrieve instructions on demand, which means some of the script may not exist until the malware is already running. The problem is that traditional controls can miss these kinds of attacks, and defenders may not be paying close attention to their AI services. These signals can be correlated across endpoints and network activity, but they usually occur outside of normal business hours, so organizations need the ability to investigate and respond continuously with 24×7 detection.

Practice Before You Need It

Teams that have already worked through their response process generally spend less time figuring out roles, decisions, and communications when a real incident occurs. Leaders need to regularly schedule tabletop exercises built around AI-driven scenarios, especially as new offensive capabilities go live, and test how their team handles a fast-moving attack, like a ransomware precursor or a large data theft. Security leaders also need to confirm that they have an incident response partner ready to engage quickly when something happens.

Building Resilience at Machine Speed

The fundamentals of security haven’t changed. Organizations still need strong identity controls, visibility into their environment, tested response plans, and the ability to detect suspicious behavior quickly. What has changed is the speed at which attackers can operate. As AI continues to compress the time between compromise and impact, security teams need to make sure their people, processes, and technology can keep up.

That’s why Arctic Wolf has built the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and the Aurora Agentic SOC. Our approach has always been grounded in helping organizations operationalize the fundamentals of security. That means maintaining visibility across their environment, strengthening identity security, continuously monitoring for signs of compromise, and ensuring skilled responders are ready when an incident occurs.

The addition of AI and agentic capabilities allows us to help customers execute those tasks faster and at greater scale, and our 2026 Agentic Security Operations Report outlines the impact we’ve measured. Over the past year of the Aurora Agentic SOC, investigation volume has increased 21%, while alert volume has been reduced by 19%, and we’ve shortened the time from an alert-generating event to an actionable ticket by 36%.

At the same time, agentic AI now resolves 60% of investigations, allowing human analysts to provide oversight when necessary. As attackers increasingly use AI to identify exposures, move laterally, and accelerate their operations, we’re delivering the technology designed to help defenders rapidly understand their environment, prioritize risk, investigate suspicious activity, and take action before a threat turns into a business disruption.

The future of security operations will be defined by how effectively organizations combine machine-speed analysis with human oversight. Organizations that can pair strong security fundamentals with trusted AI-driven operations will be best positioned to reduce risk, respond faster, and build resilience against the next generation of threats.

1 Attribution reflects Arctic Wolf Labs’ assessment as of the report period and may evolve with new evidence. References to threat actor identity, nexus, and intent are analytical judgments, not statements of legal fact.

articles.title: How Artificial Intelligence (AI) Can Increase Threat Detection and Response
articles.context: They are used in cybersecurity for malware classification, spam and phishing detection, fraud scoring, and vulnerability exploit prediction
articles.full_text:
Security leaders are being squeezed from both sides. On one side, threat actors are scaling operations with AI automation, using it to craft more convincing social engineering attacks, accelerating reconnaissance, and improving lateral movement.

On the other side, defenders are drowning in telemetry, suffering under staffing constraints, and facing the harsh reality that threat actors don’t keep business hours. Arctic Wolf’s 2025 Security Operations Report revealed that 51% of alerts occurred outside of business hours, with 15% striking on the weekend — as attackers know this is when organizations’ security teams are most likely to be understaffed.

But defenders can leverage AI for their advantage, as well. Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming foundational to modern threat detection, investigation, and response (TDIR). When done right, AI doesn’t replace human experts. Instead, it compresses the TDIR timeline, shrinking the window between noticing something strange and doing something about it. At scale, AI can turn an environment of overwhelming raw signals into a manageable number of high-fidelity security alerts, and then help IT and security teams respond consistently and effectively.

In the 2026 Arctic Wolf Threat Report, ransomware, business email compromise (BEC) and data incidents accounted for 92% of our incident response engagements, with data-only extortion surging a stunning 11% year over year. This is a clear signal that identity environments and remote access tools are a primary target for threat actors, as they shift to a “log in” rather than a “break in” operating model, using valid credentials and unpatched vulnerabilities as a simple, straightforward path to access. With these techniques able to blend in with standard traffic, defenders need to supercharge their detection and response — and that’s where AI comes in.

What Are the Core AI Technologies Used in Cybersecurity?

Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to a single control domain within cybersecurity. It is being applied across:

Attack surface management

Identity governance

Fraud prevention

Vulnerability prioritization

Cloud security posture management

Security operations.

Whether the objective is reducing false positives in an email spam filter, prioritizing the remediation of exploitable vulnerabilities, or rapidly identifying lateral movement in a hybrid environment, the underlying AI building blocks are often the same.

For security leaders, the key is to separate marketing claims from architectural reality. “AI-powered” must translate into specific analytic techniques, data dependencies, and operational workflows. When we narrow the focus down from cybersecurity broadly to threat detection, investigation, and response (TDIR) specifically, these core AI technologies become the engine that drives scalable, high-fidelity security operations.

Here are some of the core AI methodologies underpinning modern, advanced cybersecurity platforms and, more specifically, TDIR.

Supervised Machine Learning

Supervised ML models are trained on labeled datasets — for example, “malicious vs. benign” — to classify events, files, domains, processes, or behaviors. They are used in cybersecurity for malware classification, spam and phishing detection, fraud scoring, and vulnerability exploit prediction. When it comes to TDIR, supervised machine learning models are used for

High-volume alert classification

Known attack pattern detection

Commodity TTP recognition (e.g., common ransomware behaviors)

Unsupervised and semi-supervised ML models are also used to identify anomalies, which is essential in environments where there is a risk of attackers “living off the land” and using legitimate tools or valid credentials to evade signature-based controls.

Behavioral Analytics

AI models can establish a baseline of “normal” activity across users, endpoints, services, and workloads, detecting deviations over time. AI Behavioral analytics models are used in cybersecurity for identity and access monitoring, privileged access oversight, and SaaS usage governance. Within TDIR, they’re used to:

Detect impossible travel or abnormal login patterns

Catch unusual administrative behavior

Find data access anomalies and lateral movement indicators

Graph Analytics

Graph-based models represent entities — users, hosts, IP addresses, applications and processes — and their relationships as interconnected nodes. This structure enables analysis of connections across multiple points (multi-hop analysis) and relationship discovery that linear log analysis can’t easily achieve. In modern cybersecurity, graph analytics are used to detect fraud rings and insider collusion, analyze identity entitlement, and map supply chain risks. In TDIR, they’re used to:

Correlate weak signals into a cohesive incident

Map lateral movement paths

Connect identity abuse to downstream impact

Enhance investigation workflows, where scope expansion and relationship mapping are critical

Large Language Models (LLMs)

LLMs enable rapid summarization, deeper contextual interpretation, and guided workflows. In cybersecurity, they’re commonly used to enhance threat intelligence, accelerate policy analysis, and generate risk reports. When used within TDIR, LLMs can:

Provide incident summarization

Generate alert narratives

Provide analysts assistance during investigations

Offer structured playbook guidance and documentation

It’s clear that artificial intelligence is reshaping the cybersecurity industry and improving TDIR solutions. Let’s take a closer look at TDIR, and how AI is transforming the practice of security operations.

What Is AI-Powered Threat Detection and Response?

AI-powered TDIR is a modern, proactive cybersecurity methodology that applies advanced artificial intelligence, machine learning (ML), and automation to continuously detect, analyze, and remediate threats at machine speed — far faster and more accurately than traditional, manually driven security operations.

Applying AI to the full detection-to-response lifecycle can improve the entire TDIR process in meaningful ways:

Detection: Rapid identification of suspicious or malicious activity across environments (including endpoints, identities, networks, cloud environments and SaaS), by spotting behavioral anomalies, correlating weak signals, and reducing false positives

Investigation: Enrichment and connection of events into an incident narrative, mapping to attacker tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) and prioritizing based on potential impact

Response: Recommending or automating containment and remediation actions like disabling accounts, and supporting consistent execution and documentation

In practice, however, AI TDIR is not a single model. It’s an overall architecture covering data pipelines, analytics, model governance, human-in-the-loop validation, and workflow automation — all engineered to perform consistently under real-world conditions and constraints.

How Does AI-Powered Threat Detection Work?

At its most simple and succinct, AI-powered threat detection works by combining scale, context, and probabilistic reasoning in a number of ways:

Ingest and Normalize Telemetry

Security-relevant signals come from identity providers, endpoints, networks, cloud control planes, email, and SaaS. The hard part isn’t collecting logs; it’s making them comparable and queryable at speed, which AI can help with.

Reduce Noise Through Multi-Stage Filtering

A realistic pipeline for this looks like:

Data quality checks: Timestamps, schema validation, and deduplication

Rule-based screening: Known-bad indicators of compromise and policy violations

Statistical / ML scoring: Anomaly and risk signals

Correlation into higher-order detections: Joining weak signals into an incident

In the modern threat landscape, scale matters. The Arctic Wolf 2025 Security Operations Report found that the Aurora Platform, reduced 330 trillion raw observations down to 8.6 million alerts for a noise reduction rate of over 99.9%, or 1 real alert per 138 million observations.

Enrich Detection with Context

Raw detections, no matter how accurate the model, lack meaning without business and environmental contest. AI increases detection fidelity by layering contextual intelligence that converts anomalies into prioritized, detection-ready insights. Artificial intelligence can improve fidelity when it has the proper context:

Validate with Human Expertise

High-stakes security decisions made within TDIR need human oversight, both for efficacy and efficiency. The Aurora Platform uses AI to accelerate triage and investigation, while expert analysts validate alerts, determine scope, and drive response. And it’s highly effective at scale. Alpha AI triaged 10% of alerts for our customers in the past 12 months, eliminating over 860,000 manual reviews, contributing to a 37% decrease in mean time to ticket (MTTT).

How To Leverage AI Across the TDIR Stack

AI delivers the most value when it’s applied end-to-end, not tacked onto a single tool.

Detection:

Behavioral anomaly detection for identity abuse like impossible travel, atypical OAuth consent and unusual admin activity

Endpoint analytics for living-off-the-land commands and suspicious process trees

Email threat detection to catch AI-generated social engineering at scale

This last point is especially important, as our data finds that phishing drove 85% of BEC incidents responded to by Arctic Wolf Incident Response in the past year. AI is helping these attacks grow in scale and become more convincing.

Investigation:

Automated incident stitching that links alerts into a single narrative

Entity relationship mapping for graph-based scope expansion

LLM-assisted summarization

Mapping activity to common intrusion paths like remote access abuse, credential misuse or lateral movement

Our 2026 Threat Report found that 65% of non-BEC intrusions stemmed from the abuse of remote access products and services like Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), VPN, and RMM tools, reflecting attacker preferences for easy remote access paths over complex exploits.

Response:

Decision support like recommended actions based on observed techniques

Workflow automation for ticket creation, evidence capture, and coordination across teams

Containment actions like account disablement, endpoint isolation, and blocking malicious domains

Recovery:

AI-assisted reporting on timelines, affected assets, and actions taken

Control gap analysis to determine where the attack could have been stopped earlier

Continuous detection engineering based on novel TTPs observed in the wild

What Are the Benefits of AI-Enhanced Cyber Threat Detection?

The question is not whether AI is “innovative” but whether it measurably improves detection fidelity, investigation speed, and response precision across real-world attack scenarios. Here are a few of the major benefits AI provides to IT and security leaders, free of the marketing speak:

Noise Reduction

Modern security environments generate billions or even trillions of telemetry events across identity, endpoint, cloud, SaaS, and network layers. The limiting factor is not visibility — it is how many alerts human experts can realistically review. AI can help reduce noise through:

Multi-stage filtering

Collapsing multiple weak signals into a single detection

Duplicate suppression and alert clustering

Contextual risk weighting by privilege, asset tier and exposure

This scale of reduction can:

Lower false-positive rates

Reduce alert fatigue

Improve analyst retention

Improve signal-to-noise ratio

Faster Triage and Investigation

Acceleration in early-stage investigations can directly impact and reduce containment timelines and bring about faster triage in a number of ways:

Pre-correlating related events into incident clusters

Enriching alerts with identity, asset, and threat intelligence context

Providing baseline comparisons like peer group deviations and historical norms

Generating structured incident summaries

Surfacing affected entities faster

Helping to identify likely root cause sequences

Highlighting probable ATT&CK tactics

Recommending next steps for human-led investigations

These actions, when configured correctly and managed by human experts, can reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR), speed containment actions, provide more consistent investigation workflows and improve adherence to service level agreements.

Improved Detection of Credential-Based Attacks

Modern intrusions frequently rely on legitimate credentials and remote access tools. When leveraged properly in modern security operations, AI-powered behavioral baselines can help human experts detect:

Abnormal authentication patterns

Privilege escalation inconsistent with user role

Lateral movement across identity and endpoint telemetry

These types of signals are often invisible to static, signature-based controls like legacy antivirus and firewalls because the activity blends into normal traffic. It’s only through the application of the types of behavioral context shown above that modern credential-based attacks can be caught early enough to minimize impact.

Greater Resilience Against Modern Extortion Models

As mentioned earlier, our reporting found an 11x increase year over year in data incidents where exfiltration was the primary extortion driver, not encryption. As the modern ransomware model evolves, it’s more important than ever for organizations to have rapid detection and scoping capabilities. AI can improve this resilience by:

Identifying suspicious data access or staging behavior earlier in the kill chain

Correlating exfiltration signs across systems

Accelerating containment before leverage escalates

Stronger Human Decisions

AI enhances — but cannot replace — analyst expertise. However, by surfacing contextual evidence faster, mapping attack techniques, and standardizing investigation workflows, AI can support more consistent and defensible decisions. Arctic Wolf’s Navigating the Human—AI Relationship for Security Operations Success found that 99% of surveyed IT and security leaders expect the presence or absence of AI in tools and solutions to influence their cybersecurity purchases or renewals over the next 12 months. Still, the objective is not automation for its own sake, but rather faster, more confident human-led security operations.

What Are the Challenges of AI-Enhanced Cyber Threat Detection?

AI does not eliminate operational risk, it distributes it across data engineering, model governance, automation controls, and human trust. For security leaders, understanding the challenges of AI is essential to deploying it for threat detection and response safely and effectively.

Data Quality and Coverage Gaps

AI systems are downstream of telemetry. If data is incomplete, inconsistent, or poorly normalized, model output can degrade. Effective AI-powered TDIR requires disciplined telemetry engineering for log validation, health monitoring, enrichment standardization, and explicit visibility metrics like the percent of endpoints reporting or the percent of privileged accounts fully logged.

Model Drift and Environmental Change

Behavioral models assume that “normal” has statistical stability. In real environments, “normal” shifts constantly with SaaS adoption or migration, mergers and acquisitions which introduce new identity domains, changes in workforce size or distribution, and infrastructure changes like a move to the cloud. Operationally mature AI programs will implement the following to mitigate this drift:

Rolling baselines with decay weighting

Drift detection metrics like feature variance and distribution shift alerts

Regular red-team validation against known ATT&CK techniques

Human expert review of model performance trends

Explainability and Trust

Security decisions have business impact. Isolating a production server or disabling an executive’s account requires reasons security teams can defend. This kind of explainability is not optional in modern TDIR—it is foundational to adoption and safe response execution. Without it, AI introduces two major forms of operational risk:

Bypass risk, where analysts ignore AI because they don’t trust it

Automation risk, where teams place too much trust on opaque AI models and execute disruptive actions without proper scrutiny.

Privacy, Bias, and Governance

AI processes high-volume identity, behavioral, and potentially sensitive data. However, it must operate within auditable, policy-driven controls — especially in highly regulated industries. From a technical standpoint, AI presents the following challenges to privacy, bias and governance:

Data residency and cross-border log aggregation

LLM prompt leakage risks

Retention policy conflicts

Role-based access controls for AI outputs

Bias in anomaly detection across user populations or geographies

Over-Reliance on Automation

AI automation can accelerate response, but unless it’s properly configured, it can impact operations in a number of high-risk ways:

Automatic account lockouts triggering executive access outages

Endpoint isolation on critical infrastructure systems

Bulk firewall blocks affecting production traffic

Automated remediation misclassifying legitimate administrative activity

What Are Best Practices for Implementing AI-Powered TDIR?

If you’re implementing artificial intelligence into your threat detection, investigation, and response, these are the best practices that separate durable outcomes from ineffective security operations — whether internal, vendor-led, or hybrid:

Start With a Threat Model and Use-Case Backlog

Prioritize what matters: identity compromise, remote access abuse, BEC, and ransomware precursors

Engineer Your Telemetry Like a Product

Define minimum viable logging for identity, endpoint, network, and cloud

Validate log integrity and time sync

Treat parsing and normalization as first-class engineering

Measure the Right Outcomes

MTTD/MTTT/MTTR

Percentage of alerts automatically triaged

False-positive rate on high severity alerts

Time-to-containment speed for priority scenarios

Insist on Humans in the Loop

Use AI for acceleration

Require human validation for disruptive actions like account lockouts or network isolation

Constrain LLM Usage

Use retrieval-based designs grounded in telemetry outputs and approved knowledge

Prevent sensitive data leakage via policy and technical controls

Ensure log prompts and outputs are verifiable

Secure 24×7 Security Operations

Threat actors consistently attack off-hours, which means you must have detection and response capabilities that work as well at 2 a.m. on Saturday as they do at 2 p.m. on Monday

FAQ

How does AI improve threat detection?

AI improves threat detection by learning what normal activity looks like across users, devices, and applications. It then flags behavior that doesn’t fit. AI connects weak signals from endpoint, identity, network, and cloud data into a single incident and filters out noise. At Arctic Wolf®, AI speeds up detection while our security experts validate alerts and lead response.

How is AI threat detection different from signature-based detection?

Signature-based tools match activity against known threats. AI models look at behavior, so they can flag new malware or attacker techniques that don’t match a known signature. This matters most for credential-based attacks, where intruders use valid logins and legitimate tools to blend in.

Does AI replace security analysts?

No. AI handles high-volume triage, correlation, and summarization so analysts can focus on real threats. Experts still validate alerts, determine scope, and approve disruptive actions like account lockouts or network isolation.

How does AI reduce false positives and alert fatigue?

AI filters telemetry in stages, removes duplicate alerts, and combines related weak signals into one incident. Analysts see fewer alerts with more context already attached.

How does Arctic Wolf use AI for threat detection?

Aurora® Managed Detection and Response (MDR) applies AI to endpoint, identity, network, and cloud data on the Aurora Superintelligence Platform. Our Concierge Security® Team validates alerts and guides response.

How Arctic Wolf Leverages AI in Managed Security Operations

AI is reshaping cybersecurity and the landscape of threat detection, investigation, and response because the math of security operations has changed. Threat actors are scaling, telemetry volumes are exploding, off-hours attacks have become routine, and extortion models are evolving beyond encryption toward exfiltration.

The answer isn’t more alerts or more tools. It’s the ability to make better decisions faster. As the pioneer of the first open XDR platform, the Arctic Wolf Aurora™ Platform leverages AI to enable cyber defense at an unprecedented capacity and scale — processing over 10 trillion events per week ,and enriching them with threat intelligence and risk context to drive faster threat detection, simplify incident response, and eliminate alert fatigue.

Explore how generative and agentic AI, large-scale data lakes, and human expertise are converging to power a new era of security operations in our on-demand webinar, Operationalizing the AI-Powered SOC.

articles.full_text:
In April, Arctic Wolf Labs documented how BlueNoroff used fake Zoom and Microsoft Teams meetings, ClickFix prompts, and AI-generated participants to compromise leaders in the Web3 and cryptocurrency sector. We expected the threat actor to adapt after we published that report. Instead, BlueNoroff spent the next six months meticulously changing almost every red-flag “tell” a target can see, but changed almost nothing about how the intrusion itself works.

Now, the fake meeting is no longer the lure. Through access to the threat actor’s own infrastructure, Arctic Wolf tracked BlueNoroff expanding its operation into the everyday workflows of crypto and venture-capital professionals. New lures have been set up to target high-ranking targets such as founders, CEOs and senior executives, in the form of shared financial documents, PDF viewer updates, fake media players, identity verification prompts, hardware-wallet access, and security audit workflows.

This blog offers a brief overview of our findings. Full details of our investigations into BlueNoroff’s latest campaign tactics can be found in our new white paper on the topic.

What’s Inside the Full Report

A tour of BlueNoroff’s lure factory. New lure themes we uncovered appeared as custom artwork, operator guides, and test scripts in the actor’s media library before going live. We walk you through one end to end: a fabricated media player named NovaStream that progressed from AI-generated artwork to a fully operational malicious delivery kit.

Same trick, new pretext. Every lure still follows the same pattern. The threat actor establishes professional trust with the intended target, manufactures a technical problem, and persuades the target to run a “fix” that retrieves the next stage of the attack.

A wider net, with leadership the primary target. The number of individuals we identified in BlueNoroff’s media library grew from roughly 400 (of which we independently verified 100 in our April report), to 677 individuals across 58 countries. Founders and C-suite executives make up 84% of that total. These counts describe who the threat actor prepared material against, not confirmed compromises.

Custom guides help targets compromise themselves. BlueNoroff crafts “helpful” instruction videos that walk targets past browser warnings and through unfamiliar macOS and Windows workflows.

AI as a production multiplier. Generative AI now supplies attackers with platform artwork, avatars, and realistic synthetic participant video at a much higher volume and degree of realism. We show how we identified deepfakes using provenance evidence rather than visual inspection, and why AI sped up the operation.

New infrastructure with familiar habits. The BlueNoroff campaign moved to a coordinated cluster of servers, but its naming conventions, delivery commands, and certificate habits tie it directly back to the April activity. We document 98 high-confidence domains, 73 of which had not been previously reported.

How to protect yourself and your organization. We provide a robust Appendix of tips for defenders, including detection opportunities, MITRE ATT&CK® information, YARA rules, and a full list of Indicators of Compromise (IOCs).

Meet BlueNoroff

Back in April, our Adversary Operations team identified and tracked BlueNoroff activity as part of our ongoing threat research investigations. During that process, we uncovered infrastructure, targeting patterns, and operational tactics associated with the group’s campaigns, and realized we had something larger on our hands.

BlueNoroff is a financially motivated subgroup of North Korea’s Lazarus Group, publicly attributed to the DPRK’s Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB). The group has been active since at least 2014 and is highly focused on revenue generation through theft of cryptocurrency and financial assets. BlueNoroff primarily targets individuals with access to, or influence over digital assets, particularly those who have authority and trust, and uses social engineering techniques to gain access to systems, credentials, and digital assets.

In more recent years, the group’s activity has been heavily focused on the Web3 and digital asset ecosystem, and the latest campaign Arctic Wolf observed tells its own story along well-worn lines.

How BlueNoroff Helps Targets Compromise Themselves

We’ve all been there: we’re about to hop on a long-awaited Zoom call with a peer or a prospect when the audio breaks, or the video connection fails. Our blood pressure and stress levels rise as we search for a “quick fix.” That very human response is what BlueNoroff counts on, so they can covertly hand targets the means to infect themselves: a popup that we might expect to see appear while having technical troubles, with helpful instructions that guide the target through running commands or clicking buttons they might ordinarily think twice about interacting with.

The BlueNoroff Cycle of Compromise

In our April report, we showed how BlueNoroff secretly recorded the live webcams of targeted individuals as they tried to fix a fake Teams or Zoom call with no audio. What the targets didn’t know was that all the other “participants” on the call were either deepfakes, static profile pictures scraped from the internet, or pre-recorded stolen footage from other people they knew. As they tried unsuccessfully to fix the call’s audio, their own accounts were covertly compromised and plundered for contacts.

Each newly compromised target yielded real video material to populate future fake meetings, plus contacts for BlueNoroff to reach out to others in the target’s professional circle.

BlueNoroff’s foundational social engineering cycle.

What’s New in This Campaign

Over the last six months or so, Arctic Wolf Labs observed a significant evolution in both the scale and the complexity of this operation. Back in April, through access to the threat actor’s media library, we identified 400+ targets (100 of whom we independently verified) spread over 20 countries. In more recent months, we’ve identified 677 targets across 58 countries, and observed through continuing access to that same media library that BlueNoroff’s social engineering pipeline has changed at both ends.

Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate. Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims’ webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person’s likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves.

BlueNoroff’s updated attack flow (Click to enlarge).

Manipulated Media

Downstream, the “recycling” loop that turns compromised victims into material for the next scam has sped up and improved. By November 2026, production had moved from one editor on one laptop using Adobe Premiere to create basic deepfakes (which we documented back in April), to a full chain of generative AI-based services. BlueNoroff is now using and combining legitimate tools including Google Generative AI, Grok Imagine, Wondershare AIGC and GPT-4o to create a more mature editing workflow, and the videos they produce can no longer be distinguished from genuine webcam footage by visual inspection alone.

As a result, we based all deepfake determinations on provenance evidence rather than appearance. Arctic Wolf uses the U.S. Government Accountability Office definition of a deepfake: video, audio, or imagery generated or manipulated with AI to create, replace, or alter a person’s likeness or synthesize speech. Media edited exclusively with legitimate production tools such as Adobe Premiere Pro, Microsoft Clipchamp, or Wondershare without an observed generative AI step was classified as manually manipulated content rather than a deepfake.

Our forensic analysis of 349 videos in BlueNoroff’s media library flagged as “likely modified” as of November 6. A video with several signatures appears in several ribbons (Click to enlarge).

New Lure Themes

Instead of relying on their previous “fake meeting” ruse, BlueNoroff now leverages multiple lure themes to socially engineer targets and deliver payloads through platform-specific workflows. Although the branding, content, and delivery mechanisms varied, each lure followed the same underlying pattern. The document-themed lures we observed used several related pretexts: a protected file could not be decrypted, a shared document required verification, or the browser’s PDF viewer needed an update.

One of the platform-specific lures we observed used a fake Chrome PDF Viewer that claimed that Chrome’s built-in PDF component could not display a document without an update. Selecting “Update Now” initiated an AppleScript download in the recovered macOS flow. Windows and Linux users were instructed to execute commands that retrieved a payload from a fake Chrome update site set up by the threat actor.

After execution, the page displayed a Chrome-branded “Update Complete” dialog, reproducing the false-success mechanism observed in the earlier fake-meeting intrusions.

Fake Chrome update popup lure created by BlueNoroff. Clicking “Update now” initiates an AppleScript download.

Conclusion

BlueNoroff’s new lures and intrusion scenarios (painted in more detail in our full report) align closely with common workflows in venture fundraising and digital-asset investment, where pitch decks, investment agreements, and restricted documents move between founders, investors, and advisers. By aligning lures with fundraising, investment, scheduling, media, wallet, and security workflows, BlueNoroff places malicious execution inside activities that targets routinely perform.

Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff’s efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships.

While AI is now being used as production multiplier that helps BlueNoroff scale and diversify, it has not fundamentally changed the intrusion mechanism. The campaign still remains dependent on target research, operator engagement, tailored infrastructure, and manual user execution.

Why it Matters

Individual brands, domains, and visuals used as lures by attackers will keep changing. The step they all depend on remains the same: a trusted-looking page asks the target to run something locally, which most often involves a manual step like clicking a button on a popup. That behavior is the most reliable place to disrupt this campaign, and our report includes the detection logic, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, YARA rules, and indicators of compromise to help defenders protect their organizations against these types of social engineering attacks.

The TL;DR takeaway: treat any request to run a command, script, shortcut, or workflow as a red flag, however polished the interaction looks, and confirm unusual requests through a separate, out-of-band known-good channel.

Get the full analysis, detections, and indicators. Download the full report (PDF).

How Arctic Wolf Protects Its Customers

Arctic Wolf is committed to ending cyber risk, and when active campaigns are identified, we move quickly to protect our customers. We have leveraged threat intelligence around this threat activity to enhance detections in the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora® Endpoint Security, subject to customer environment and available telemetry. Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Detection and Response (MDR) provides detection for the PowerShell, curl-piped and osascript execution patterns plus the process-injection and persistence techniques documented in our April report, and the network indicators in our November report.

As this campaign develops, Arctic Wolf may refine detections for additional indicators of compromise and techniques leveraged by this threat.

Recommended Mitigations

While no organization is immune from social engineering attacks, there are steps that can be taken to minimize the likelihood of an intruder succeeding in gaining a foothold. While BlueNoroff’s campaign may seem sophisticated, their attack chain goes nowhere when their intended victim exercises basic security hygiene.

We recommend the following additional mitigations:

Verify unexpected requests. Organizations should focus on teaching employees at every level of the company to exercise caution around unexpected requests of all types, which strengthens internal defenses against social engineering. Train employees to independently verify meeting invitations and identity verification requests through a separate trusted channel.

Beware of third parties bearing gifts. Be wary of “helpful” materials sent by an external contact, particularly PDFs and links to videos and other recordings, even those that seem legitimate or contain known/trusted company and brand names.

Beware of scams that involve fake “fixes.” Be particularly cautious of requests to install software, run scripts, or execute commands, especially during meetings, videos, phone calls, and other seemingly personal interactions that create a sense of urgency.

Provide deepfake training. Train employees to recognize modern social engineering techniques, including the use of AI-generated content and deepfakes by those seeking access to company credentials. For those without the time or resources to create their own training program, the Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness® training solution includes content on fake-meeting and ClickFix social engineering, including a “Report Phish” button.

Recognize leadership as the primary target set. C-suite executives and founders account for 84% of identified targets in the BlueNoroff campaign we observed. Implement strong authentication and access controls for high-risk users, including executives and employees with access to company finances or digital assets.

About Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence enables organizations to leverage the same intelligence that powers the Arctic Wolf Security Operations Center (SOC), delivering real-time data on emerging threats. With curated reporting and real-time threat campaign notifications, businesses stay informed and increase prevention without needing to sift through vast amounts of information.

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence leverages over 8 trillion weekly security observations across 10,000+ customers, spanning industries and geographies, and provides actionable insights in an easy-to-digest format even outside Arctic Wolf. With IoC QuickLinks into Data Explorer, customers can rapidly check their environments for active threats, and take swift action to mitigate risks.

The insights generated can be automatically operationalized across Security Operations technologies, including EDR, SIEM, and network security controls, leveraging industry-standard integrations such as STIX/TAXII and dynamic blocklist APIs to accelerate detection and response. Arctic Wolf’s Threat Intelligence solution is available as an MDR add-on or a standalone deliverable.

Additional Arctic Wolf Resources:

Read our April report on BlueNoroff: BlueNoroff Uses ClickFix, Fileless PowerShell, and AI-Generated Fake Zoom Meetings to Target Web3 Sector
